title: Raga Majh
hook: a raga with Punjabi folk roots (ang 94), full of longing

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Sri Rag, and your line was which watch now. What did the hour answer when you asked? Today, the second raga on the list. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

Some ragas sound like a palace. This one, tradition says, sounds like a village. In the heart of the Punjab, between the Beas and the Ravi rivers, lies the country called the Majha, and Sikh tradition links the raga's name to that land and its songs. Turn to ang ninety-four of the Guru Granth Sahib and there it is, right after Sri Rag, at the head of its own long section. Today: Raga Majh.
screen: `A PALACE, OR A VILLAGE?` → `THE MAJHA, BETWEEN TWO RIVERS.` → `ANG 94: RAGA MAJH.`

segments.voice: Majh is a raga with dust on its feet. Some musicians say it grew from the folk singing of the Punjab rather than from the old classical treatises, and that its home is the field and the courtyard more than the court. Whatever its exact road, the mood tradition hears in it is longing: a voice calling across a distance, to someone who isn't here yet. Call it the sound of missing. So it's fitting where the Gurus set it, second, right after Sri Rag's gravity. Open the section and the first hymn isn't Guru Nanak's. It's Guru Ram Das's. It begins, in paraphrase: the Lord's Name has become dear to my mind; by great good fortune I've come to meditate on it. Already the language is the language of love. A thing becomes dear. Fortune brings it near. And the section keeps going: hymns of Guru Amar Das, of Guru Arjan, and Guru Nanak's var in Majh, a long ballad of stanzas and saloks. Why would the Gurus take a raga with country roots into scripture, and put it near the front? The Granth doesn't explain its choices. But the effect is easy to hear. The divine isn't only praised in the grand voice of Sri Rag. It's also longed for in the plain voice of home, in the tune of a song someone might sing while working, missing a person far away. A listener who grew up with that sound can hear scripture in their own accent. That's today's line: punjabi longing. Tomorrow, one hymn in Majh, and the longing gets a story.
screen: `MAJH: A RAGA WITH DUST ON ITS FEET.` · `THE MOOD: LONGING ACROSS A DISTANCE.` · `IT OPENS WITH GURU RAM DAS.` · then, large: `PUNJABI LONGING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Majh. If you can find a shabad sung in Raag Majh, play it now. Before you follow the words, listen for the reaching in the melody, the way a phrase leans out toward something and comes back. If you can't find one, bring to mind someone you miss: far away, out of touch, or gone. Don't push the feeling up or down. Just let the missing sit beside you for a minute, the way a song sits beside the one who sings it. If you pray, you can hold that person, and the longing itself, inside one quiet Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Raga Majh. The second raga section of the Granth, opening on ang ninety-four with Guru Ram Das, named by tradition for a region of the Punjab, and heard as a raga of longing. Today's word.
Your line: punjabi longing. Today, send one short message to someone you miss, and keep it plain, in the words you'd say at home. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Ragis sing shabads from the Majh section in Raag Majh, and its compositions, including Guru Nanak's Majh ki Var, are read in the Guru Granth Sahib in the order the Granth gives them.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Majh, the raga of the Granth's second section; tradition links it to the Majha region of the Punjab.

trapdoor: what you thought: Majh is one more classical raga.
what it means: a raga tradition ties to the Punjab's own country, heard as longing, set second in the Granth.

what a scholar hears: the Majh section (from Ang 94) opens with Guru Ram Das's chaupade, includes Guru Amar Das's ashtapadis, Guru Arjan's hymns and Guru Nanak's Majh ki Var; some musicologists trace the raga to Punjabi folk melody rather than the older classical texts.
